title: Archipenko Waited Forty-Seven Years to See This Dancer Cast in Bronze
standfirst: The plaster was modelled in Paris in 1913, then left in storage in Europe while its maker built a new career, a new citizenship and a new fame in America. By the time it finally became metal, the date stamped on its surface had stopped being the most interesting thing about it.

sections.heading: It's Inscribed 1913. Nobody Poured Bronze Until Decades Later
sections.body: Sotheby's own catalogue entry for one numbered cast of this sculpture records what is stamped into its surface: the name "Archipenko," the date "13," and an edition mark, "8/8F." Every bronze cast under this title carries that same incised year, 1913 — the year Archipenko modelled the plaster in Paris. None of them were cast that year. The [Archipenko Foundation's own chronology](https://www.archipenko.org/life-and-work.html) records the return of his early plasters, "stored in the South of France since c. 1921," arriving only in 1960, when Archipenko travelled to France, tracked down work he had not seen in decades, shipped it to New York and began casting it into bronze in his seventies. He died in February 1964 with the edition unfinished. The remaining casts, [Sotheby's provenance notes state](https://www.sothebys.com/en/auctions/ecatalogue/2017/impressionist-modern-art-evening-sale-n09710/lot.11.html), were "finished after his death in 1964 under the authority of his estate." What is dated 1913 on the surface of this object is the idea behind it. The metal is a different age entirely.

sections.heading: The Same Dancer Stands in More Than One Museum
sections.body: Because the edition was poured in batches, this exact title exists as more than one bronze, with more than one account of its own dates. The [Archipenko Foundation's own inventory](https://www.archipenko.org/life-and-work.html) lists a "Blue Dancer," dated 1913, held at the Saarlandmuseum in Saarbrücken, Germany. The [North Carolina Museum of Art's cast](https://learn.ncartmuseum.org/artwork/blue-dancer/), bought with state purchase funds, stands 41 inches high with a blue patina on a marble base and is catalogued as "modeled 1913 to 1918; cast after 1961" — five years of uncertainty folded into the word "modeled" alone. [Sotheby's cast](https://www.sothebys.com/en/auctions/ecatalogue/2017/impressionist-modern-art-evening-sale-n09710/lot.11.html), numbered 8/8F, measures 105.8 centimetres and, per the house's own account, had its casting "begun under the artist's supervision" in 1960. Three institutions, three separate castings — and not one of them disagrees about the date on the bronze, because that date was never really describing the bronze.

sections.heading: Paris in 1913 Could Not Stop Watching People Dance
sections.body: Archipenko had been in Paris since 1908, working through years when the city's avant-garde treated dance as a subject worth returning to constantly. Henri Matisse's La Danse, a panel of five dancing figures, had its [first public showing at the 1910 Salon d'Automne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dance_%28Matisse%29) before it went to Moscow as a commission for the collector Sergei Shchukin. Archipenko's own dance sculptures multiplied in the years after: "Médrano I" in 1912, built from wood, glass and metal wire and named for the Montmartre circus where much of the avant-garde spent its evenings, and this bronze's own immediate predecessor, a work called Red Dance, modelled in 1912–13. Dance wasn't a subject Archipenko chose once — it was the subject nearly everyone around him kept choosing that decade, and this figure, mid-balance on its toes, is his particular answer to a question the whole city was asking.

sections.heading: He Insisted He Was First. The Record Around Him Says "Almost"
sections.body: Archipenko joined the Salon Cubists just after the 1910 Salon d'Automne, where the proximity of [other artists' paintings](https://www.theartstory.org/movement/salon-cubism/) reportedly pulled in Roger de la Fresnaye and a second sculptor, the Hungarian-born [Joseph Csaky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Csaky). By 1911 both were showing Cubist sculpture at the Salon des Indépendants alongside Duchamp, Gleizes, Léger and Metzinger; by October 1912 both were exhibiting as members of the Section d'Or at the Galerie La Boétie, alongside Raymond Duchamp-Villon and de la Fresnaye again. The critic Michel Seuphor later put a plain order on the two of them: "Csaky, after Archipenko, was the first sculptor to join the cubists." Csaky, for his part, reportedly stood closer to Archipenko personally than to Picasso or Apollinaire, despite having met both. On one narrower claim, though, there is less argument: in 1932 the Bauhaus artist László Moholy-Nagy credited Archipenko in print with "the first conscious use of concaves in sculpture – to replace saliences," a deviation that pushed the viewer, he wrote, toward "the elementary possibilities of the positive-negative relations." Five years later it was Moholy-Nagy who invited Archipenko to Chicago to head the modelling workshop at the New Bauhaus.

sections.heading: The Same Year Chicago Hired Him, Germany Called His Work Degenerate
sections.body: 1937 cut two ways. In Chicago, Moholy-Nagy's New Bauhaus gave Archipenko a faculty post and a fresh audience. In Germany, where he had lived, exhibited and taught through the early 1920s, Nazi authorities confiscated his sculptures as "Degenerate Art" — a seizure confirmed independently by both the Archipenko Foundation's own chronology and the [North Carolina Museum of Art](https://learn.ncartmuseum.org/artwork/blue-dancer/), which notes only that it took in "many of Archipenko's sculptures that were on display in German museums," without naming which. Archipenko had emigrated to New York in October 1923, arriving on the SS Mongolia and declaring, without much modesty, that "America is the only country not jaded and rent by war." The plaster for this dancer, though, had already been left behind even earlier — in the south of France, not Germany, since around 1921 by his own foundation's account. Work made in one place, in one decade, kept resurfacing somewhere else, on somebody else's schedule, long after Archipenko had moved on. He died in New York on 25 February 1964, according to his foundation "shortly after casting his last bronze": a [smaller prototype](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Archipenko) for what became the 14.5-foot King Solomon, left unfinished at his death and completed by his widow, Frances Archipenko Gray, in 1968. She was also, per Sotheby's own provenance record, the first owner of this particular casting after his death — it passed from her to Perls Galleries in New York in 1965, to the collector Evelyn Sharp by 1968, into the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum as part of the Sharp collection in 1978, and through a Sotheby's saleroom in 1997 to its present, unnamed owner. The plaster took forty-seven years to become a bronze. The bronze has been quietly changing hands for longer than that ever since.
